copy: SWE-EVO: what your agent harness still needs

Newer frontier models can need less behavioral scaffolding. Your repository still needs clear constraints, useful context and evidence that a change works. Here is how to decide what to remove—and what to keep.
· Co-authored with AI · First published 2 February 2026 · 9 min read
When you upgrade the model, re-test the instructions you inherited.
Remove duplicated advice and old workarounds in measured steps. Preserve the requirements that define a correct change, and enforce critical boundaries through tools and checks.
Start with one recurring task: compare your current prompt with a lean version on the same repository commit. Judge the patch before judging the token count.
The instructions that helped yesterday can get in the way today

Long prompts accumulated for understandable reasons: they corrected behaviors a model repeatedly got wrong. A model upgrade changes that tradeoff. A blanket rule about comments, a prescribed planning ritual or several examples of the same tool call may constrain a model that can now make those decisions itself.

, Anthropic says it removed over 80% of Claude Code’s system prompt for advanced models, including Opus 5 and Fable 5, without measurable loss on its coding evaluations. It describes conflicting instructions across context layers and moving review and verification guidance into selectively loaded skills.

also recommends removing repetition and simplifying tool descriptions, with internal evaluation results favoring leaner configurations. Both are vendor findings under their own conditions. Neither establishes that every tool is removing instructions, or that every long prompt harms every model.
treat inherited process instructions as hypotheses to re-test. Keep the information that makes your task different from generic coding work.
Give each instruction a reason and a place
Read the assembled context, including system instructions, repository files, skills and tool descriptions. A short
can still be redundant if several other layers repeat it. A longer task reference can be valuable when it supplies information the model cannot otherwise know.
Duplicated advice, obsolete workarounds and rules that no longer fix a measured failure.
The requested behavior, compatibility requirements, repository-specific traps and exact validation commands.
Specialist procedures and detailed references needed for this task, through a discoverable skill or document.
Permissions, schema validation, protected branches and release gates through executable controls.

Practitioner framework — aictrl editorial guidance. These are decisions to evaluate, not measured performance rankings. A reminder can accompany a control; the control must work when the reminder is missed.

For example, “be a careful engineer” gives little local information. “This API must still accept the old field name until the next major release” defines a concrete obligation. A skill can describe the migration procedure. A compatibility test can detect when the obligation is broken.
The research does not support deleting all repository context

found that generated context files did not significantly improve task resolution and increased average inference cost by 20% on SWE-bench and 23% on CTXbench. Developer-written files performed better than generated files, but their improvement over no context file was not statistically significant in that study.
study of 124 pull requests across ten repositories

with lower median runtime and output-token use. These studies use different tasks and measures. Together, they argue for testing your actual context and workload rather than using file length as a quality score.
SWE-EVO shows why the harness still needs an evaluation

SWE-EVO tests release-to-release changes: 48 tasks across seven Python projects, averaging about 21 edited files and 874 tests. Resolution requires the requested changes without regressions; Fix Rate captures partial progress while penalizing regressions. See
. Published results, not an aictrl evaluation.
The same model can produce different results with another harness.
This comparison does not isolate prompt length:
tools, orchestration and other configuration differences also change. SWE-EVO supports evaluating the whole setup; it does not prove that adding or removing instructions caused the differences.

Readout limits: the paper’s headline maximum conflicts with Table 2; we use the named table rows. One resolved task changes the rate by about 2.08 percentage points. This is a small, Python-only dataset, not a current universal ranking. Claude and Gemini are absent from that table.

For your team, the question is whether the agent can carry a change across the contracts your repository actually has. A passing unit test in one file is incomplete evidence if the API, persistence schema or client still disagrees.
A small system prompt can still carry a large tool catalog

measured six released CLIs with a local scripted model. In aictrl 0.5.4, the system prompt accounted for 608 reference tokens. Its nine tool definitions added 2,772. The larger opportunity in that configuration was the tool surface.
Measured overhead — five single-response captures per configuration, median first-request estimates using
. These are offline reference counts, not provider-billed usage.

Restricting aictrl to the same four tool types used by pi—read, write, edit and shell—removed 1,351 estimated tokens from the first request. It also exposed instructions that still referred to tools we had disabled. That is a concrete audit target: make the instructions match the tools actually available to the run.

scoping the available tools reduced request overhead in this experiment. We cannot conclude that it improved coding quality, saved a particular billed amount or required fewer model turns. The scripted model did not solve a software task. See the

examine domain-rule compliance under no-skill, Markdown and pseudocode conditions. They ask a different question from release completion. We do not treat those older configurations or their rule scores as evidence about today’s frontier-model prompt removal.
Run a small ablation before rewriting every instruction

Choose a recurring change with a verifiable outcome. For example: rename an API field while retaining support for its old name. The agent must update the public response, validation, storage mapping, client and documentation, while keeping existing clients working. This is a proposed exercise, not a measured aictrl result.
Write the outcome before prescribing the process
Replace vague pressure and a generic sequence of steps with the behavior and evidence you need. The following is an editorial example; substitute your actual contract and commands.
Be extremely careful. Always make a detailed plan. Read every related file. Follow all best practices. Think step by step and check your work repeatedly.

Expose displayName in the API and client. Keep accepting name from existing clients during migration. Do not change authorization or remove stored data. Use this repository's documented validation commands. Return the patch, checks run and any unresolved failures.
Repository instructions still supply the exact commands and non-obvious constraints. The lean version removes generic coaching, not the definition of success.
Record the repository commit, model identifier, reasoning setting, agent version, permissions, tools and run budget. Start each run from a clean disposable checkout.

A uses the current instructions. B removes duplicated advice and legacy process rules, preserving requirements. C uses B plus the relevant specialist skill. Keep tools fixed for this comparison; test tool scoping separately.

Write acceptance and regression checks before the runs; keep held-out checks outside the agent’s view. Verify old and new clients, data preservation and authorization. Review the patch for scope and security.
Report whole-task passes, regressions, elapsed time, token usage, actual cost when available, retries and human repairs. Repeated runs across several tasks provide a pilot, not a universal ranking.

Adopt the leaner condition only if it meets your predeclared quality bar. A saving that introduces a compatibility regression is a failed trade. If removing a rule causes a repeatable failure, restore the smallest instruction that addresses it and keep the failure as a regression case.
Turn the next bug into evidence for one better control
A missed requirement is an opportunity to learn where the workflow broke. Before adding another permanent paragraph to the system prompt, classify the failure and make the remedy testable.
Practitioner framework — suggested diagnoses and interventions, not experimental results.
Agent missed an undocumented compatibility rule
Add the specific constraint to repository context.
A failing compatibility test that passes after the repair.
Make the relevant skill discoverable and load it for this task.
The loaded skill version and completed procedure checks.
Align the prompt and tool catalog.
The actual request and tool-call error before and after.
Agent skipped a required validation or boundary
Put the check or permission gate in the execution path.
A controlled failure showing the gate blocks completion.

On the next model upgrade, replay these cases. Retire workarounds that no longer help; retain requirements and controls whose purpose still exists. That gives the instruction library a maintenance loop instead of allowing it to grow after every incident.
Keep the patch, the configuration and the proof together

Pick one change and compare the three instruction conditions before choosing a new default. Keep its failing runs as carefully as its successful ones. The useful output is a decision about your workload, with enough evidence for someone else to challenge it.
